content: Glomerales is an order of symbiotic fungi that belongs to the phylum Glomeromycota. These fungi are obligate biotrophic mutualists, meaning they rely on a symbiotic relationship with a host organism for survival. Most members of this order utilize the arbuscular mycorrhizal (AM) method to exchange nutrients with plants. This involves the formation of specialized structures called arbuscules within plant root cells, facilitating the transfer of essential nutrients such as phosphorus to the plant and carbohydrates to the fungus. The fungi in this order produce large spores, often exceeding 5 mm in diameter. These spores, which include azygospores and chlamydospores, are multinucleate, containing thousands of nuclei within a single spore. Historically, all members of the phylum Glomeromycota were thought to be closely related to the fungal family Endogonaceae. However, molecular sequencing data has revealed that they are more closely related to the Dikarya, a subkingdom of fungi that includes the Ascomycota and Basidiomycota. Fossil evidence indicates that members of this order have existed since the Ordovician period, approximately 460 million years ago, making them one of the oldest known fungal lineages. The family name Glomeraceae, which serves as the basis for the order name Glomerales, was historically misspelled as Glomaceae, leading to the incorrect spelling of the order as Glomales. These errors are correctable under the rules of the International Code of Botanical Nomenclature, which standardizes the naming of plants and fungi. Unfortunately, the incorrect spellings are still frequently encountered in scientific literature.
